harrisons_synthesis: Clinical syndrome resulting from structural or functional cardiac impairment that reduces ventricular filling or ejection
Left-sided failure manifests as dyspnea, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea due to pulmonary congestion
Right-sided failure presents with jugular venous distension, hepatomegaly, and peripheral edema
Reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF, EF ≤40%) vs preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF, EF ≥50%) guide treatment strategy
BNP and NT-proBNP are key biomarkers for diagnosis and prognostication
treatment_pearls: Guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) includes ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2i
ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) superior to ACEi alone in reducing mortality in HFrEF
Loop diuretics for volume management — titrate to euvolemia, not a fixed dose
ICD indicated for primary prevention when EF ≤35% despite 3 months of GDMT
Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) when LBBB with QRS ≥150ms

harrisons_synthesis: Spectrum including unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI caused by acute atherosclerotic plaque disruption
STEMI defined by persistent ST-elevation ≥1mm in ≥2 contiguous leads with troponin rise
Chest pain radiating to the left arm or jaw, diaphoresis, and nausea are classic but may be absent in diabetics and elderly
Acute plaque rupture exposes subendothelial collagen triggering platelet aggregation and thrombus formation
Killip classification grades hemodynamic severity from I (no heart failure) to IV (cardiogenic shock)
treatment_pearls: Door-to-balloon time <90 minutes for primary PCI in STEMI is the critical quality metric
Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT): aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor preferred over clopidogrel)
High-intensity statin therapy initiated regardless of baseline LDL
Beta-blockers within 24h if no contraindications (cardiogenic shock, bradycardia, decompensated HF)
Anticoagulation with heparin (UFH or enoxaparin) during acute management

harrisons_synthesis: Characterized by insulin resistance in peripheral tissues and progressive pancreatic β-cell dysfunction
Presents with polyuria, polydipsia, blurred vision, fatigue, and recurrent infections
HbA1c ≥6.5%, fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL, or 2-hour OGTT ≥200 mg/dL confirms diagnosis
Microvascular complications include retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy — onset correlates with duration and glycemic control
Macrovascular disease (CAD, CVA, PAD) is the leading cause of mortality in T2DM
treatment_pearls: Metformin remains first-line pharmacotherapy — reduces hepatic glucose output
SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) provide cardiorenal protective benefits beyond glycemic control
GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide) preferred in patients with atherosclerotic CVD or obesity
Annual screening: dilated eye exam, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, monofilament foot exam
Insulin therapy indicated when HbA1c remains above target despite maximal oral/injectable therapy

harrisons_synthesis: Progressive airflow limitation that is not fully reversible, caused by chronic inflammatory response to noxious particles
Emphysema (parenchymal destruction) and chronic bronchitis (productive cough ≥3 months/year for 2 consecutive years) are the two classic phenotypes
Spirometry showing post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 confirms obstruction
GOLD staging based on FEV1 % predicted: Stage I (≥80%), II (50-79%), III (30-49%), IV (<30%)
Acute exacerbations (AECOPD) are triggered by viral/bacterial infections and are the major driver of morbidity
treatment_pearls: Smoking cessation is the only intervention proven to alter the natural history of COPD
Inhaled bronchodilators (LABA + LAMA combination) are the cornerstone of maintenance therapy
Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) added for patients with frequent exacerbations and eosinophil count ≥300
Supplemental O2 when resting PaO2 ≤55 mmHg or SaO2 ≤88% — improves survival
Pulmonary rehabilitation reduces dyspnea and improves exercise capacity in all GOLD stages

harrisons_synthesis: End-stage of chronic liver injury characterized by diffuse fibrosis, regenerative nodules, and architectural distortion
Common etiologies: alcohol-associated liver disease, chronic hepatitis B/C, and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD)
Compensated cirrhosis may be asymptomatic; decompensation manifests as ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, or jaundice
Portal hypertension (HVPG ≥10 mmHg) drives most complications — esophageal varices, splenomegaly, ascites
Child-Pugh and MELD scores are used for prognostication and transplant listing prioritization
treatment_pearls: Non-selective beta-blockers (carvedilol or nadolol) for primary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding when varices ≥5mm
Lactulose and rifaximin are first-line for prevention and treatment of hepatic encephalopathy
Diagnostic paracentesis mandatory for new-onset ascites — SBP if PMN ≥250/μL
Hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance: ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months
Liver transplantation evaluation when MELD ≥15 or first decompensating event

harrisons_synthesis: Defined as abnormalities in kidney structure or function present for >3 months with health implications
Diabetes and hypertension account for >60% of CKD cases in developed nations
Uremia syndrome in advanced CKD includes nausea, pericarditis, encephalopathy, and bleeding diathesis
CKD-mineral bone disorder (CKD-MBD) involves hyperphosphatemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and renal osteodystrophy
treatment_pearls: ACEi/ARB are first-line for reducing proteinuria and slowing CKD progression — monitor K+ and creatinine
SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin) reduce CKD progression independent of diabetes status
Blood pressure target <130/80 mmHg; tighter control if proteinuria >1 g/day
Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESA) for anemia when Hb <10 — target 10-11.5 g/dL
Renal replacement therapy planning (dialysis access or transplant referral) when eGFR <20

harrisons_synthesis: Obstruction of pulmonary arterial vasculature by thrombus, most commonly originating from deep veins of the lower extremities
Classic triad of dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and hemoptysis is present in <20% of cases
Massive PE causes acute right ventricular failure and hemodynamic collapse
CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the diagnostic standard — sensitivity >95%
Wells score and D-dimer guide pre-test probability assessment and diagnostic pathway
treatment_pearls: Systemic anticoagulation with heparin ± transition to DOAC (rivaroxaban, apixaban) is standard of care
Systemic thrombolysis (alteplase) indicated for massive PE with hemodynamic instability
Catheter-directed therapy for submassive PE with RV dysfunction remains an evolving option
IVC filter only when anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated (active hemorrhage)
Extended anticoagulation (>3 months) for unprovoked PE — risk-benefit reassessment at 3-6 months

harrisons_synthesis: Acute loss of focal neurological function lasting >24 hours due to vascular occlusion in a defined arterial territory
Large vessel atherosclerosis, cardioembolism (atrial fibrillation), and small vessel lacunar disease are the major subtypes
NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) quantifies deficit severity and guides treatment eligibility
Diffusion-weighted MRI is most sensitive for acute ischemia — CT primarily excludes hemorrhage
Penumbra concept: ischemic tissue surrounding the core infarct is salvageable with rapid reperfusion
treatment_pearls: IV alteplase within 4.5 hours of symptom onset — door-to-needle time <60 min target
Mechanical thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion up to 24 hours (with perfusion imaging selection)
Permissive hypertension in acute stroke — do NOT lower BP unless >220/120 (or >185/110 if thrombolysis candidate)
Secondary prevention: antiplatelet (aspirin + clopidogrel short-term), statin, and risk factor modification
Atrial fibrillation-related stroke requires anticoagulation (DOAC preferred over warfarin)

harrisons_synthesis: Acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma presenting with cough, fever, dyspnea, and radiographic infiltrate
Streptococcus pneumoniae remains the most common identified pathogen; atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Legionella) also prevalent
Severity stratified by CURB-65 or PSI scores to guide inpatient vs outpatient management
Parapneumonic effusions develop in 20-40% of hospitalized cases — thoracentesis if >10mm on lateral decubitus
Complications include empyema, lung abscess, and ARDS in severe cases
treatment_pearls: Outpatient: amoxicillin or doxycycline; macrolide if atypical coverage needed
Inpatient (non-ICU): beta-lactam + macrolide OR respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy
ICU admission: beta-lactam + macrolide (or fluoroquinolone); add vancomycin/piperacillin if MRSA/Pseudomonas risk
Dexamethasone 6mg × 4 days may reduce mortality in severe CAP requiring ICU care
Follow-up chest radiograph at 6-8 weeks in smokers and patients >50 to exclude underlying malignancy

harrisons_synthesis: Sustained systolic BP ≥130 mmHg or diastolic BP ≥80 mmHg (ACC/AHA 2017 guidelines)
Essential (primary) hypertension accounts for 90-95% of cases; secondary causes include renal artery stenosis, pheochromocytoma, and primary aldosteronism
Silent end-organ damage includes LVH, CKD, retinopathy, and subclinical cerebrovascular disease
Hypertensive emergency: BP >180/120 with acute end-organ damage (encephalopathy, aortic dissection, acute HF)
White-coat and masked hypertension diagnosed via 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM)
treatment_pearls: First-line agents: ACEi/ARB, calcium channel blocker, thiazide diuretic — choice guided by comorbidities
Black patients without CKD: CCB or thiazide preferred over ACEi/ARB as initial monotherapy
Resistant hypertension (uncontrolled on 3 drugs including diuretic): add spironolactone 25-50 mg
Hypertensive emergency: IV nicardipine or clevidipine — reduce MAP by 25% in first hour, NOT to normal
Lifestyle: DASH diet, sodium <2.3g/day, 150 min/week aerobic exercise, weight loss of 1 kg ≈ 1 mmHg reduction

pathophysiology: Acute kidney injury involves a rapid decline in glomerular filtration rate leading to the retention of nitrogenous solutes. The underlying mechanism can be prerenal due to inadequate systemic perfusion, intrinsic due to tubular injury from sepsis or nephrotoxins, or postrenal from urinary tract obstruction.
clinical_presentation: Patients typically present with a reduction in urine output (oliguria or anuria) and fluid retention. Signs of uremia including mental status changes, bleeding complications, and profound volume overload may also manifest.
diagnostics: Diagnosis requires an elevation in serum creatinine from baseline or a documented reduction in urine output. Urine sediment examination, serum cystatin C, renal ultrasound to rule out obstruction, and occasionally a kidney biopsy are utilized.
treatment_and_management: Management involves optimization of systemic hemodynamics, careful volume resuscitation, and immediate elimination of nephrotoxic agents. Continuous renal replacement therapy or hemodialysis may be necessary for severe or refractory cases.
prognosis_or_complications: Life-threatening hyperkalemia, marked volume overload, metabolic acidosis, and progression to chronic kidney disease.

pathophysiology: CKD is characterized by initiating damage followed by a nonspecific, maladaptive hyperfiltration and hypertrophy of the remaining viable nephrons. Over time, increased intrarenal renin-angiotensin activity leads to glomerular architecture distortion, podocyte dysfunction, and progressive nephron sclerosis.
clinical_presentation: Early stages are typically asymptomatic, but progressive decline leads to fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, edema, sensory polyneuropathy, and sleep disorders. In advanced stages, the uremic syndrome manifests with severe hypertension, encephalopathy, pericarditis, and asterixis.
diagnostics: Diagnosis relies on an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 or a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio greater than 30 mg/g persisting for at least 3 months. Renal ultrasound typically reveals bilaterally small kidneys with cortical thinning.
treatment_and_management: Treatment includes tight blood pressure control (<130/80 mmHg), renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (ACE inhibitors or ARBs), and SGLT-2 inhibitors to slow disease progression. Dietary protein and salt restriction are recommended, with renal replacement therapy (dialysis or transplant) indicated for end-stage disease.
prognosis_or_complications: Progression to end-stage renal disease (ESRD), significantly increased risk of cardiovascular disease, anemia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

pathophysiology: Heart failure results from structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling or ejection, causing elevated intracardiac pressures and inadequate peripheral oxygen delivery. It involves a complex progressive cycle of maladaptive ventricular remodeling, often driven by continuous neurohormonal activation following an initial myocardial injury.
clinical_presentation: Cardinal symptoms include breathlessness, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fatigue, and reduced exercise capacity. Physical signs consist of elevated jugular venous pressure, pulmonary crackles, an S3 gallop, and dependent peripheral edema.
diagnostics: Echocardiography is the primary noninvasive modality used to assess ventricular structure, valvular function, and ejection fraction. Elevated circulating levels of B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) or NT-proBNP strongly support the diagnosis, alongside a 12-lead ECG and chest x-ray.
treatment_and_management: Foundational pharmacotherapy includes renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system antagonists (ACEIs, ARBs, or ARNIs), beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and SGLT-2 inhibitors. Loop diuretics are used to manage congestion, while implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) are considered for sudden death prevention.
prognosis_or_complications: Acute decompensated heart failure requiring repeated hospitalizations, cardiogenic shock, and high risk of sudden cardiac death from ventricular arrhythmias.

pathophysiology: Ischemic heart disease develops when there is an imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand, most commonly due to atherosclerotic narrowing of the epicardial coronary arteries. This obstructive disease causes a regional reduction in myocardial blood flow and inadequate tissue perfusion.
clinical_presentation: Patients classically present with typical angina pectoris, consisting of exertional chest discomfort, pressure, or heaviness. Women frequently present with atypical symptoms such as fatigue, anxiety, nausea, indigestion, and upper back pain.
diagnostics: The diagnosis is supported by 12-lead electrocardiography at rest and during standardized exercise stress testing. Advanced imaging modalities like stress echocardiography, radionuclide myocardial perfusion imaging, and coronary CT angiography are used, with invasive coronary arteriography remaining the gold standard.
treatment_and_management: Medical therapy relies on organic nitrates, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, and SGLT-2 inhibitors to control anginal symptoms. Revascularization with percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) is indicated for severe refractory symptoms or high-risk anatomy.
prognosis_or_complications: Unstable angina, acute myocardial infarction, and progressive left ventricular dysfunction culminating in ischemic cardiomyopathy.

pathophysiology: COPD is characterized by persistent airflow obstruction caused by a combination of small airway disease and emphysematous parenchymal destruction. Inhalation of noxious particles, usually cigarette smoke, incites chronic inflammation, goblet cell hyperplasia, and proteolytic degradation of elastic fibers in the distal airways and alveoli.
clinical_presentation: Patients present with a chronic productive cough, progressive exertional dyspnea, and an increased effort to breathe. Physical examination often reveals a prolonged expiratory phase, expiratory wheezing, hyperinflation causing a barrel chest, and use of accessory respiratory muscles.
diagnostics: Spirometry is absolutely required for diagnosis, demonstrating a persistent and irreversible reduction in the FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.70. Chest CT is used to definitively establish the presence, specific pattern, and extent of emphysematous changes.
treatment_and_management: Management centers on smoking cessation and the use of inhaled bronchodilators, primarily long-acting muscarinic antagonists and long-acting beta-agonists. Inhaled corticosteroids are added for patients with frequent exacerbations and elevated blood eosinophils, while continuous supplemental oxygen improves survival in those with severe resting hypoxemia.
prognosis_or_complications: Acute respiratory exacerbations, frequent respiratory tract infections, and the development of pulmonary hypertension leading to right heart failure (cor pulmonale).
